title: Dead while alive
hookLine: Kabir speaks of dying to ego while still living, and so being free

cards: Some people go quiet when the subject of dying comes up. Change the topic. Knock on wood.
Kabir does something stranger. He talks about death as if it were good news. Not someday, at the end, but now, while the heart is still beating.
For two days he's been lowering himself: the worst of all, the Lord's dog. Today we find out where that road goes. It goes somewhere that sounds, at first, like a contradiction.

teach.b: Here's one of Kabir's saloks. The dying that the world fears, he says, brings joy to my mind, because it's through dying that perfect bliss is found. Kabir isn't longing for a funeral.
Sikh readers hear in this a different death: the death of the ego, the I that grabs and compares and insists on its own way.
Haumai, Sikhs call it, the sense of I, me, mine. It's what kept a proud man sure his birth made him higher, and what points at everyone else's faults. This week's hymns have been slowly loosening it.
When it finally lets go, something is left that's lighter and freer, and still breathing. That's today's word. Jeevan mukat.
Jeevan is life. Mukat is freedom, release.
Free while living. Sikh teaching doesn't place freedom only after death, in some far-off place. It can be tasted here, at the kitchen sink, at the loom, in traffic.
The person who's free while living still works, still eats, still loves their family. Kabir kept singing. What has died is the grip.
Picture holding a hot pan by the handle, knuckles white, scared to drop it. Now set it down. Your hand is still your hand; it's just not clenched anymore.

teach.h: THE CLENCH GOES, THE HAND STAYS.
teach.b: The clench goes, the hand stays.
So the line we carry out of this week isn't about the end of life. It's about the middle of it.

how: Sikhs speak of jeevan mukat as freedom from ego while living an ordinary householder's life, and Kabir's saloks on dying to the self are sung and explained in kirtan and katha.

o: freedom that comes only after death
free while living, released from ego's grip
a long life free of any hardship

games.q: dead while alive — tap the pairs.

s: in this salok, Kabir is longing for his own funeral
Sikh readers hear the death of ego, not of the body.
jeevan mukat means free while living
jeevan is life, mukat is freedom.
someone free while living stops working and leaves their family
they still work, eat and love their family. what's gone is the grip.

games.q: you're Kabir. the whole world fears dying. you want to sing about it. what do you say?
o: it's the worst thing; avoid the subject.
the dying the world fears brings joy to my mind.
games.why: Kabir says that dying brings joy, because through it perfect bliss is found. Sikh readers hear the death of ego while still alive.

practice: Find one small thing your I is gripping right now: the last word, the credit, someone noticing you were right.
Don't fight it; just name it, and on each out-breath loosen your hold by a little, like setting down a hot pan, and see what's left. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each out-breath.

wordCard.voice: Jeevan mukat. Free while living: released from the grip of ego here and now, not only after death.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: liberated while living, free from ego here and now.

carryVoice: Your line: free while living. A week with Kabir ends in the middle of life, hands open. Rest well.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Salok Kabir, Ang 1365 ('the dying the world fears brings joy to my mind; through dying, perfect bliss is found')
